summary: Bay after bay of beaches, Nelson's dockyard, and Barbuda's pink sand and frigatebirds.
overview: Antigua, the larger of the two islands, has a coast so cut with bays that Antiguans like to say there's a beach for every day of the year. Dickenson Bay and Runaway Bay lie close to St John's in the north-west, Half Moon Bay faces the Atlantic in the east, and Darkwood and the long beaches of the south-west look towards Montserrat. Inland the island is low and dry, dotted with the stone towers of old sugar mills; at Betty's Hope one has been restored with its sails, and Fig Tree Drive winds through the greener hills of the south, below Mount Obama, the highest point at 402 m.

English Harbour, on the south coast, is the place most visitors remember. Nelson's Dockyard, the Royal Navy's Georgian base, has been restored as a working marina and is a World Heritage Site, and above it the lookout at Shirley Heights has a long-running Sunday afternoon party with a steel band and a barbecue. St John's, the capital, is where the cruise ships dock, with a busy market and a white cathedral with twin towers. Minibuses run from the capital's bus stations, but most visitors use taxis or a hire car, driving on the left on narrow, bumpy roads.

Barbuda, a flat island to the north, is reached by ferry or a small plane. It has long empty beaches with a pink tint from crushed shells, and a frigatebird colony in Codrington Lagoon, one of the largest in the Caribbean, best seen from a boat in the nesting months of autumn and winter. Hurricane Irma badly damaged the island in 2017.

seasons.name: Sunny season
seasons.text: Low humidity, steady trade winds and very little rain. This is the sailing season too: superyachts fill the harbours in winter, and the regattas come in April and early May. Book Christmas and Sailing Week well ahead.

seasons.name: High summer
seasons.text: Hot and more humid, with passing showers and a growing chance of tropical storms. Carnival fills St John's at the end of July and the start of August.

seasons.name: Peak of the hurricane season
seasons.text: September and October carry the highest risk of storms and are the wettest months. Some restaurants and hotels shut for a few weeks around September; November is quieter, greener and usually drier.

whenToGo.weather: Antigua is one of the drier islands of the eastern Caribbean, with roughly 1,000 mm of rain in an average year and long dry spells; much of the island's water comes from desalination. Daytime temperatures run from about 28°C in January to 31°C in August, and nights rarely fall below 22°C. The trade wind blows from the east most of the year, which is why the island draws so many sailors. Barbuda is flatter and drier still.

festivals.name: Antigua Classic Yacht Regatta
festivals.text: Wooden schooners, ketches and other classic yachts race off the south coast, with a parade of sail through the harbour.

festivals.name: Antigua Sailing Week
festivals.when: Usually late April into early May
festivals.text: One of the Caribbean's best-known regattas, held since 1968: racing by day and crowded bars around the dockyard by night.

festivals.name: Antigua Carnival
festivals.when: Usually from late July to the first Tuesday of August
festivals.text: Celebrates the end of slavery in 1834, with calypso and soca contests, a pageant, J'ouvert before dawn on Carnival Monday and the costumed bands parading through the capital on the Monday and Tuesday.

festivals.name: Independence Day
festivals.text: A public holiday marking independence from Britain in 1981, with a ceremonial parade and events in the days around it.

regions.name: Antigua
regions.text: Nearly all the hotels, restaurants and sights, and the yachting harbours of the south coast.

regions.name: Barbuda
regions.text: Quiet, with one village, Codrington, and few visitors. Best as a day trip or a short stay for the beaches and the frigatebirds, in the calm, dry months.

culture.greetings: Start every exchange with a greeting for the time of day: Antiguans take it as basic good manners, and skipping it is the quickest way to seem rude. A handshake is usual between strangers, and friends often bump fists. Older people may be addressed as Mr or Miss followed by their first name.
etiquette: Wearing camouflage-pattern clothing is against the law for anyone who isn't in the armed forces, children's clothes included: leave it at home.
Barbuda's frigatebird colony is visited by boat with a local guide: keep your distance from the nests.
Water is precious on a dry island that relies on desalination, so keep showers short.
Ask before taking photographs of people, including vendors at the market.
The roads have potholes, sharp bends and few signs: drive slowly, and take a taxi home from the Sunday party at Shirley Heights.
culture.tipping: About 10% is the norm in restaurants, but many already put it on the bill as a service charge. Guides and boat crews on day trips expect something, and taxi fares can be rounded up.
culture.dress: Light, loose clothes and a hat. Smart casual in the evening at the dockyard's restaurants. Leave camouflage prints behind (see above), and pack a light layer for breezy boat trips.

food.name: Fungee and pepperpot
food.text: The national dish: fungee is cornmeal cooked with okra and shaped into a smooth ball, and pepperpot a thick stew of salted meat, spinach, aubergine and squash.

food.name: Ducana and saltfish
food.text: Ducana is grated sweet potato with coconut, sugar and spice, wrapped in a banana leaf and boiled. It's served beside stewed saltfish, a pairing found on most local menus.

food.name: Antigua Black pineapple
food.text: A small, very sweet pineapple grown on the island for centuries. Look for it at the market in St John's and in fresh juices.

food.name: Wadadli and local rum
food.text: Wadadli is the island's own lager, and the Antigua Distillery makes English Harbour and Cavalier rums, poured neat or in a rum punch.

phrases.intro: Antiguans use English at school, at work and in government. At home and among friends they speak Antiguan Creole, which can be hard to follow at first. A few words:

items.meaning: Good morning: say it when you walk into a shop, a bus or a bar
Antigua's old Amerindian name, and the local beer
A street party with music and dancing
Carnival costume, and the bands that parade in it

items.text: Eastern Caribbean dollar (EC$, XCD). US dollars are widely accepted, though change usually comes in EC dollars.
English. Antiguan Creole is spoken day to day.
items.note: Wikidata also lists Spanish as an official language. English is the language of government; Spanish is spoken by a minority with roots elsewhere in the Caribbean and Latin America, so the page leaves it out.
